```{r appendix-setup}
# Appendices A-C. Knit as a child of journal-paper.Rmd (after the references,

# Summary of Experimental Conditions

Table \ref{tab:app-conditions} describes the `r length(xsl_datasets)` experimental conditions included in the model comparison, including the number of trials, the number of words presented per trial (Words/Trial), the number of referents presented per trial (Objects/Trial), the number of to-be-learned word-referent pairs (Items), people's overall mean accuracy ($p(o|w)$ across all intended $w-o$ mappings) in each condition (Accuracy), the standard deviation of performance (SD), and the number of participants per condition (N).

```{r conditions-table, results="asis", echo=F}
# NOTE (revision): repointed at XSLmodels::xsl_datasets (53 conditions) in
# place of the frozen 44-condition data/combined_data.RData. Words/trial and
# objects/trial are constant within every condition (verified separately),
# so the first trial's count is used.
tab <- purrr::map_dfr(xsl_datasets, function(d) {
  tibble(
    "Condition Name" = d$condition,
    "Trials" = length(d$train$words),
    "Words/Trial" = length(d$train$words[[1]]),
    "Objects/Trial" = length(d$train$objects[[1]]),
    "Items" = length(d$accuracy),
    "Accuracy" = mean(d$accuracy),
    "SD" = sd(d$accuracy),
    "N" = d$n_subj
  )
})

app_tab_cond <- xtable::xtable(tab, digits=2, label = "tab:app-conditions",
                       caption = "Summary of modeled datasets.")

print(app_tab_cond, type="latex", comment = F, include.rownames = F, table.placement = "p", caption.placement = "top", size = "\\footnotesize")
```

# Model Misfit by Experimental Condition

```{r load-cv-appendix}
# CV fits come from paper/load_fits.R (sourced in the setup chunk): the v05
# refit's 5-fold CV over the 47 conditions.
cvg_app <- cvg %>% mutate(Model = relabel(Model))
n_models_appendix <- length(unique(cvg_app$Model))

# Conditions with only a condition-level human accuracy (replicated across
# items) have no item-level variance to correlate with, so they're excluded
# from the correlation-based views below. None remain in the v05 fit set
# (Koehne et al. 2013 and Suanda et al. 2014 are held out), but the check
# stays.
zero_var_conds <- cvg_app %>% group_by(Condition) %>%
  summarize(human_sd = sd(HumanPerf), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(human_sd == 0) %>% pull(Condition)
```

The heatmap below shows cross-validated model fit (SSE; sum of squared error) for each experimental condition, across all `r n_models_appendix` fitted models and the `r length(unique(cvg_app$Condition))` conditions with cross-validated fits.
Note that each model has difficulty fitting at least one or more experimental conditions--and these difficult conditions vary somewhat by model.
For example, the strength-biased model has particular difficulty with the `filt` conditions[^filt0E] (Kachergis et al., 2012), which present a group of word-referent pairs early in training which then systematically co-occur with particular novel late-stage word-referent pairs, testing how strictly learners will maintain a mutual exclusivity (ME) constraint.
The Propose-but-Verify model also shows greater misfit in most of these conditions (except for the `filtXE_3L` conditions, which have only 3 repetitions of the late-stage pairings, and thus do not overwhelm learners' ME bias).
<!-- ToDo (revision): re-check both of these claims against the 53-condition,
     15-model heatmap below once cv_all_experiments.R finishes -- they were
     written against the original 44-condition, 11-model version. -->

On the other hand, many experimental conditions are nearly equally well fit by all models, especially those that have a fixed number of repetitions per word-referent pair (e.g., 3x3 and 4x4, although 2x2 presents difficulties for some models).

[^filt0E]: Except for the `filt0E_` conditions, which consist only of the late-stage pairs, with no early stage.

```{r app-sse-heatmap, fig.width=9, fig.height=10, out.width="100%", fig.pos="p", fig.cap="Cross-validated misfit (mean squared error per item) of each model on each experimental condition, clustered by condition (rows) and model (columns); brighter red is worse."}
exp_by_mod <- cvg_app %>%
  mutate(SSE = (ModelPerf-HumanPerf)^2) %>% # should we weight be sample size?
  group_by(Condition, Model) %>%
  summarize(meanSSE = mean(SSE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(id_cols = Condition, names_from = Model, values_from = meanSSE)

xm_mat <- as.matrix(exp_by_mod[, -1, drop = FALSE]) # all fitted models, however many
row.names(xm_mat) = exp_by_mod$Condition

colfunc <- colorRampPalette(c("black", "red"))
heatmap.2(xm_mat, col=colfunc(20), cexCol=.7, srtCol=45, margins = c(8,6.5)) # , scale="row"
```

## Correlation of Model and Human Item-Level Performance per Condition

Each cell displays the correlation coefficient of model vs. human item-level performance in a given experimental condition.
`r if (length(zero_var_conds)) paste(length(zero_var_conds), "conditions with only condition-level human accuracy are excluded here, since a correlation is undefined without item-level variance in the human data.") else ""`

```{r app-r-heatmap, fig.width=9, fig.height=10, out.width="100%", fig.pos="p", fig.cap="Item-level correlation between each model's cross-validated predictions and human accuracy, per experimental condition, clustered by condition (rows) and model (columns)."}
exp_by_mod_r <- cvg_app %>%
  filter(!Condition %in% zero_var_conds) %>%
  group_by(Condition, Model) %>%
  summarize(r = cor(ModelPerf, HumanPerf), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(id_cols = Condition, names_from = Model, values_from = r)

xm_mat <- as.matrix(exp_by_mod_r[, -1, drop = FALSE])
row.names(xm_mat) = exp_by_mod_r$Condition
heatmap.2(xm_mat, col=brewer.spectral(30), # brewer.pal(11,"RdBu")
          scale="none", trace="none",
          cexCol=.7, srtCol=45, margins = c(8,6.5)) # scale="row", "col" <- interesting
```

## Which Experimental Designs Are Easy or Hard Overall?

The heatmaps above group misfit by model; here we instead average over models, to ask which experimental designs are uniformly easy or hard to predict for *any* model -- a useful signal for choosing which conditions actually discriminate between theories, versus which conditions every model gets right (or wrong) regardless of mechanism.

```{r overall-difficulty}
exp_by_mod_long <- cvg_app %>%
  mutate(SSE = (ModelPerf - HumanPerf)^2) %>%
  group_by(Condition, Model) %>%
  summarize(SSE = mean(SSE), r = cor(ModelPerf, HumanPerf), .groups = "drop")

cond_overall <- exp_by_mod_long %>%
  group_by(Condition) %>%
  summarize(`Mean r` = mean(r, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Mean SSE` = mean(SSE, na.rm = TRUE),
            `SD SSE` = sd(SSE, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

easiest <- cond_overall %>% arrange(`Mean SSE`) %>% head(5) %>% mutate(Rank = "Easiest")
hardest <- cond_overall %>% arrange(desc(`Mean SSE`)) %>% head(5) %>% mutate(Rank = "Hardest")
extremes_tab <- bind_rows(easiest, hardest) %>% select(Rank, everything())
```

Table \ref{tab:app-extremes} shows the five conditions with the lowest mean SSE across all `r n_models_appendix` models (easiest, fit well by essentially every model) and the five with the highest (hardest, fit poorly by essentially every model).
The `SD SSE` column shows how much models disagree on a condition: a low SD alongside a high mean SSE means every model struggles with that design about equally -- a design that is hard for principled reasons rather than one that merely discriminates between theories.
<!-- ToDo (revision): once cv_all_experiments.R finishes (adding FUs), re-verify which conditions land in this table -- name the design manipulation for the hardest few explicitly in this paragraph (e.g., which filt/freq condition, contextual diversity level, or AFC condition). -->

```{r overall-difficulty-table, results="asis"}
tab_ext <- xtable::xtable(extremes_tab, digits = 3, label = "tab:app-extremes",
                          caption = "The five easiest and five hardest experimental conditions, by mean SSE across all fitted models.")
print(tab_ext, type="latex", comment = F, include.rownames = F, table.placement = "p", caption.placement = "top")
```

## Model Disagreement: A Discriminability Index Independent of Human Data

```{r model-disagreement}
gfd_group <- gfd %>% filter(Model != "fazlyt") # gfd from paper/load_fits.R; fazlyt is a group-fit-only bonus

# one representative per distinct mechanism (round 2 adds the
# reinforcement-and-inference and episodic-memory mechanisms)
mech_reps <- c("kachergis", "fazly", "Bayesian_decay", "rescorla-wagner", "trueswell2012",
              "guess-and-test", "pursuit", "softmax_rl", "kalman_filter", "tilles",
              "minerva2", "baseline")
mech_reps <- intersect(mech_reps, unique(gfd_group$Model)) # round-1 fallback lacks tilles/minerva2

item_sd <- function(df) df %>% group_by(Condition, condnum) %>%
  summarise(item_sd = sd(ModelPerf), .groups = "drop")

cond_disagree <- full_join(
  item_sd(gfd_group) %>% group_by(Condition, condnum) %>% summarise(sd_all = mean(item_sd), .groups = "drop"),
  item_sd(gfd_group %>% filter(Model %in% mech_reps)) %>%
    group_by(Condition, condnum) %>% summarise(sd_reps = mean(item_sd), .groups = "drop"),
  by = c("Condition", "condnum")
) %>% arrange(desc(sd_all))

disagree_extremes <- bind_rows(
  head(cond_disagree, 6) %>% mutate(Rank = "Most discriminative"),
  tail(cond_disagree %>% arrange(desc(sd_all)), 4) %>% mutate(Rank = "Least discriminative")
) %>% select(Rank, Condition, `SD (all models)` = sd_all, `SD (mechanism reps)` = sd_reps)

# computed here (not inline) to avoid nesting backticks (the `Mean SSE`
# column name) inside an inline r-code span, which would break knitr's parse
mean_sse_by_cond <- cond_overall %>% select(Condition, MeanSSE = `Mean SSE`)
sse_disagree_cor <- cond_disagree %>% left_join(mean_sse_by_cond, by = "Condition") %>%
  summarise(r = cor(sd_all, MeanSSE, use = "complete.obs")) %>% pull(r)
```

Mean SSE (above) indexes how *hard* a condition is, but hardness and discriminative *value* are different things: a condition every model gets equally wrong is hard but uninformative for choosing between theories, while a condition that splits the models -- whoever turns out to be right -- is exactly the kind of experiment worth running again with more power, or in a new population.
We index this directly, independent of human data, as the standard deviation of each model's predicted item-level accuracy (`ModelPerf`, at each model's group-fit parameters) across models, averaged over the items in a condition.
Because several of our associative models are one-parameter-removed cousins of each other (FU/FUs/FU-A/FU-P/Str/Unc/Nov all share the same core mechanism), their mutual spread can pad this index without reflecting genuine disagreement between *theories*.
We therefore report it two ways: across all `r length(unique(gfd_group$Model))` fitted models, and across `r length(mech_reps)` representatives, one per distinct mechanism (`r paste(relabel(mech_reps), collapse=", ")`) -- the two versions correlate at `r round(cor(cond_disagree$sd_all, cond_disagree$sd_reps), 2)`, but reorder some conditions meaningfully (see below).

Table \ref{tab:app-disagree} shows the most- and least-discriminative conditions by this measure.
The `filt9E_*`/`filt6E_*` conditions -- which present a group of pairs early, then systematically pair a subset of the late-stage objects with the early-stage words to test how strictly a mutual-exclusivity bias is maintained -- are the most model-discriminating conditions in the whole set, on both versions of the index; the temporal- and spatial-contiguity conditions also rise near the top once the FU family's internal spread is removed, indicating a genuine cross-theory split there rather than one associative model disagreeing with its own close cousins.
At the other end, `filt0E_6L`/`filt0E_9L` (the late-stage-only `filt` conditions, with no early pairs to violate) and several of the fixed-repetition `3x4`/`4x4` conditions are answered almost identically by every model regardless of mechanism -- useful as sanity checks, but uninformative for adjudicating between theories.
This index correlates with the SSE-based "hardest" ranking above at only $r \approx$ `r round(sse_disagree_cor, 2)`, confirming that "hard for everyone" and "discriminates between theories" are related but distinct properties of a design.
<!-- ToDo (revision): re-check top/bottom lists once cv_all_experiments.R finishes and FUs is added to the group-fit roster used here (group fits are already complete and don't depend on that CV run, so this section is NOT blocked on it -- only re-verify the specific numbers land the same way). -->

```{r model-disagreement-table, results="asis"}
tab_disagree <- xtable::xtable(disagree_extremes, digits = 3, label = "tab:app-disagree",
                               caption = paste0("Most- and least-discriminative experimental conditions: standard deviation of model-predicted item accuracy across models, at each model's group-fit parameters. `All models' is all ", length(unique(gfd_group$Model)), " models including the baseline; `mechanism reps' is one representative per distinct theoretical mechanism (", length(mech_reps), ")."))
print(tab_disagree, type="latex", comment = F, include.rownames = F, table.placement = "p", caption.placement = "top")
```

## Each Model's Best- and Worst-Fitting Experiment

Table \ref{tab:app-model-bw} summarizes for each model, what experimental condition is best fit by that model (in terms of correlation, `best` and `best_cond`), and what condition has the worst fit for that model (`worst` and `worst_cond`).

```{r, results="asis"}
# A handful of remaining (condition, model) pairs still have r = NA even
# after dropping the zero-human-variance conditions above -- these are
# cases where a particular MODEL's predictions happen to have zero variance
# on a particular condition (e.g. a `filt` condition where Kalman Filter
# predicts an identical value for every item), not a data problem. na.rm=T
# below just skips these for that model's best/worst; they were already a
# known quirk in the original (pre-package) version of this analysis.
exp_by_mod <- exp_by_mod_long %>% filter(!Condition %in% zero_var_conds) %>% select(Condition, Model, r)

mod_best_worst <- exp_by_mod %>% group_by(Model) %>%
  summarize(best = max(r, na.rm=T),
            worst = min(r, na.rm=T),
            best_cond = Condition[which(r==best)][1],
            worst_cond = Condition[which(r==worst)][1]) %>%
  arrange(desc(best))

most_common_best  <- names(sort(table(mod_best_worst$best_cond), decreasing = TRUE))[1]
most_common_worst <- names(sort(table(mod_best_worst$worst_cond), decreasing = TRUE))[1]
n_best  <- max(table(mod_best_worst$best_cond))
n_worst <- max(table(mod_best_worst$worst_cond))

app_tab_bw <- xtable::xtable(mod_best_worst, digits=2, label = "tab:app-model-bw",
                       caption = "Each model's best- and worst-fitting experiment.")

print(app_tab_bw, type="latex", comment = F, include.rownames = F, table.placement = "p", caption.placement = "top")
```

Across models, `r most_common_best` is most often the best-fit condition (best for `r n_best` of `r nrow(mod_best_worst)` models), and `r most_common_worst` is most often the worst-fit condition (worst for `r n_worst` models).


## Best- and Worst-Fitting Models per Experiment

Table \ref{tab:app-cond-bw} takes the complementary view: for each experimental condition, which model fits it best and which fits it worst (by item-level correlation), and then, aggregating over conditions, how many conditions each model "wins" (is the single best-fitting model for) and "loses" (is the single worst-fitting model for).
A model that wins many, varied conditions is a safe default; a model that wins a few conditions no other model wins is doing something distinctive worth understanding.

```{r, results="asis"}
cond_best_worst <- exp_by_mod %>% group_by(Condition) %>%
  summarize(best = max(r, na.rm=T),
            worst = min(r, na.rm=T),
            best_mod = Model[which(r==best)][1],
            worst_mod = Model[which(r==worst)][1]) %>%
  arrange(desc(best))

best <- cond_best_worst %>%
  group_by(best_mod) %>% summarize(best_fits = n()) %>%
  rename(Model = best_mod)

worst <- cond_best_worst %>%
  group_by(worst_mod) %>% summarize(worst_fits = n()) %>%
  rename(Model = worst_mod)

best_worst_tab <- full_join(best, worst, by = "Model") %>%
  mutate(across(c(best_fits, worst_fits), ~replace_na(., 0))) %>%
  arrange(desc(best_fits))

app_tab_cbw <- xtable::xtable(best_worst_tab, digits=0, label = "tab:app-cond-bw",
                       caption = "Number of experimental conditions that each model fits best, and worst (by item-level correlation).")

print(app_tab_cbw, type="latex", comment = F, include.rownames = F, table.placement = "p", caption.placement = "top")
```
